result.summary: Pausanias describes Phigalia: a hero-shrine in the market-place, the rivers Lymax and Neda, and the ancient temple of Eurynome with its fish-tailed statue. He then describes Mount Cotilius and the beautiful temple of Apollo the Helper at Bassæ, built by Ictinus.

scenes.title: Phigalia's market and rivers
scenes.summary: Pausanias notes the hero-shrine of the 100 men from Oresthasium and the rivers Lymax and Neda, explaining the Lymax's name from Rhea's purification.

scenes.title: Temple of Eurynome
scenes.summary: Pausanias describes the cypress-ringed temple of Eurynome, opened only once a year, and the fish-tailed statue he knows only by report. He doubts it is Artemis.

scenes.title: Cotilius and Apollo at Bassæ
scenes.summary: Pausanias describes the mountains around Phigalia, the temple of Apollo the Helper at Bassæ built by Ictinus, the spring on Cotilius and the roofless temple of Aphrodite.

alias_notes.explanation: Title Apollo got for helping Phigalia in a pestilence.
Athenian title for Apollo, for turning away a pestilence.

notable_quotes.reason: Pausanias ranks the Bassæ temple second in the Peloponnese for stone and craftsmanship.

analysis.text: Pausanias blends local cult, etymology and Homeric citation, and tests hearsay against what he has seen himself.
The Bassæ temple's link to a plague and to Ictinus reflects fifth-century dedications during the Peloponnesian War era.

legacy.text: Pausanias' praise helped bring attention to the Bassæ temple, rediscovered by travellers in 1765 and later studied for its frieze, now in the British Museum.

fun_facts.text: The Bassae temple is a UNESCO World Heritage site and is now covered by a large protective tent.

language_notes.text: A mortuary chapel is a small shrine at a burial place; the offerings are funeral rites paid annually, as to heroes (honored dead).
Lymata is a Greek word for refuse or purifications; the river's name Lymax is derived from it.
Refers to the Iliad, Book 1, where the Greeks cleanse themselves after Apollo's plague and throw the washings into the sea.
Shearing off their hair 'to the river' means cutting locks as an offering to the river-god, a common Greek custom at coming of age.
In Iliad 18, Eurynome and Thetis took in Hephæstus (the Greek smith god) when he was thrown from heaven.
Apollo 'Averter of Ill' (Alexikakos) was worshipped at Athens after the plague of the Peloponnesian War period.
The Parthenon is Athena's temple on the Athenian Acropolis, built in the time of Pericles, the statesman who led Athens.

context_notes.text: The Mæander, a river in Asia Minor, was so famously winding that the word 'meander' comes from it.
A stade was a Greek unit of length of roughly 180–200 metres, so 12 stades is about two kilometres.
Bassæ's temple of Apollo still stands and is famous for its remote mountain setting and its early use of Corinthian column design.

literary_notes.text: The dense ring of cypresses, trees associated with mourning, gives the shrine a secluded, solemn atmosphere.
Pausanias openly admits what he did not see, marking the difference between his own observation and hearsay.
Pausanias's skeptical, rationalizing habit shows as he weighs the fish-tailed image against myth and rejects the Artemis identification.
His brief, dry rebuttal of the earlier writer implies that author's claim was careless, while stressing his own firsthand checking.
